description: We are Astro Dots, a team driven by curiosity, innovation, and a passion for space exploration. We are building RED QUEST, an interactive Martian exploration and survival experience combining scientific data, immersive 3D visualization, and intelligent route planning. Our goal is to turn planetary science into an engaging journey of discovery. Together, we are pushing the boundaries of exploration beyond Earth. Our next destination: Mars!
summary: Red Quest is our proposed solution to the Martian Map challenge. It turns scattered NASA Mars data into one interactive view that helps future explorers plan and carry out a Marswalk. It has two parts. Red Map is a NASA data-driven 3D map of the Martian surface that layers terrain, elevation, hazards, resources, science targets, radiation and route information, with path-aware navigation to compare routes and discover science along the way. Red Exploration is an interactive game built on the same map, where players explore real terrain, identify geological features, and handle dust storms, communication loss and limited oxygen and energy. Together they move users from viewing Mars to making mission decisions. Next, we plan to expand coverage to Jezero Crater, integrate live REMS atmospheric weather data, simulate sand entrapment terramechanics, and introduce WebXR for immersive astronaut helmet HUD training.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

Red Quest is an interactive 3D Mars surface mapping and traverse simulation engine designed to transform raw planetary science data into an actionable navigational platform for future human extravehicular activities (EVAs) and robotic missions.

The platform combines an interactive 3D Mars globe displaying multiple planetary exploration zones with structured mission expeditions and an unconstrained Research GIS mode. In its debut expedition (Mission 01: Gale Expedition), the engine focuses on a 5 km × 5 km corridor of Mount Sharp inside Gale Crater, fusing five verified NASA datasets—USGS 1 m elevation models, HiRISE 2 m optical imagery, CRISM mineral spectra, THEMIS daytime thermal inertia, and 1,819 discrete Curiosity rover traverse waypoints—into an interactive WebGL engine.

The system operates through an intuitive 5-stage workflow (Briefing → Analyze → Choose → Explore → Debrief) and features six real-time "Decision Lenses":

• Satellite: High-resolution optical terrain context.

• Terrain: Continuous slope gradients categorized into EVA safety tiers (<15° safe, 15°–25° caution, >25° hazardous) with 25 m contour lines.

• Minerals: Orbital CRISM spectral signatures highlighting ancient aqueous clays and sulfates.

• Heat: THEMIS thermal inertia separating solid bedrock pavements from loose sandy drift traps.

• Sun & Power: Ray-marched cast shadows for Morning, Noon, and Evening solar angles.

• Radiation Shelter: 12-azimuth Sky-View Factor (SVF < 0.85) mapping terrain scarps that naturally shield astronauts from cosmic radiation.

An asynchronous A* pathfinding worker generates candidate routes (Safest, Shortest, Science-Focused) that users evaluate with a diagnostic Survey Kit, test in a 3D rover physics simulation, and benchmark against actual NASA ground truth in Debrief. Beyond Mission Mode, the platform features a free-exploration Research Mode with custom start/goal pathfinding, layer opacity sliders, and a Point Inspector.

---

Key Benefits & Intended Impact

• Bridges the Data Gap: Unifies disconnected planetary archives (topography, mineralogy, thermal, and radiation) into a single, real-time spatial interface.

• Mitigates Mission Risk: Identifies impassable scarps, soft sand traps, and solar cold spots before physical surface deployment.

• Maximizes Scientific Return: Directs astronaut traverses toward verified geochemical discoveries (smectite clays and sulfates) to optimize sample collection.

• Astronaut Health Protection: Identifies natural topographical shelters where cliff walls attenuate galactic cosmic radiation during surface operations.

• Scalable Architecture: Designed to scale across multiple planetary landing sites (with Mission 02 Jezero Crater and future planetary corridors mapped on the global interface).

• Intended Impact: Empowers future Artemis-to-Mars planners, mission scientists, and educators with an intuitive, open-source tool that makes complex extraterrestrial geography accessible and practical.

---

Creativity & Innovation

• Cognitive "Decision Lenses": Instead of static 2D map layers, operators can seamlessly toggle multi-spectral shaders over 3D terrain to inspect different physical properties of the same rock in real time.

• Dual Mode Flexibility: Bridges gamified, narrative mission planning (Briefing to Debrief) with an open-ended planetary Research GIS for custom analysis.

• Multi-Disciplinary Fusion: Combines engineering safety (slope mechanics), astrobiology (CRISM mineral indicators), space weather (radiation and solar shadows), and rover kinematics in one engine.

• Ground-Truth Validation Loop: Rather than an arbitrary game score, users' pre-lock estimates are quantitatively scored against true USGS digital elevation measurements and Curiosity's real historical path.

• Accessible Simulation: Delivers high-end planetary GIS functionality directly in a web browser without requiring heavy desktop GIS software.

---

Tools, Languages & Software Used

• Coding Languages: JavaScript (ES6+), GLSL (OpenGL Shading Language for WebGL shaders), Python, HTML5, CSS3.

• 3D & Web Frameworks: Three.js (r174) for WebGL rendering, Vite (v6.2) for bundling and local development, HTML5 Web Workers for asynchronous pathfinding.

• Geospatial & Data Processing: GDAL, Python Rasterio, Pillow, and NumPy for cropping, 16-bit heightmap normalization, and elevation validation.

• Testing & Automation: Playwright for headless browser automation and documentation capture.

• Hardware: Developed and tested on standard consumer laptops with WebGL-enabled integrated/discrete GPUs.

---

Factors & Real-World Constraints Considered

• Scientific Data Integrity: Strict adherence to verified NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) archives—zero elevation, coordinate, or spectral data was fabricated.

• Human & Mechanical Safety Tiers: Slopes are categorized based on real astronaut EVA locomotion limits and rover rollover thresholds (<15° nominal, 15°–25° slip hazard, >25° impassable cliff).

• Physical Solar & Radiation Geometry: Solar illumination is ray-marched using true Martian solar zenith and azimuth angles; radiation shielding models the thin Martian atmosphere (~6 mbar) where isotropic cosmic rays are blocked by local terrain bulk.

• Client-Side Performance: Heavy mathematical computations (A* pathfinding and slope extraction) are offloaded to Web Workers and GPU fragment shaders, ensuring a fluid 60 FPS experience with zero backend server dependencies.
